title: Explainer · Watch the Barrel (the Supply Shock Tracker)
notes: 11-05. The supply shock tracker explainer, 3–5 min (handoff 2026-11-04 §3A). Script: data/show/ex01_script_v2.md. No tape. The globe stands still on the pedestal the whole way (globe: true, globeTurn: 0); globeMonth (new, dream-news.js) holds it on the month Ted reads. Stills in ex01/stills, drawn from data/active as fetched 11-06 (August in). 11-06: tedWalk (dream-news.js) — Ted walks from the desk to the globe on q_who and stays; the picture resolves as he arrives (trackerResolveShow).

beats.text: Is more of the world's oil being sold in dollars this year, or less? That's the one thing this globe reads.
beats.caption: More dollars, or fewer?

beats.text: I scroll Twitter like everybody else. A hurricane of vibes about oil, almost no signal. So we built something that only watches the barrel. Where it goes, and what money it's paid in.
beats.caption: Watch the barrel

beats.text: I'm Ted Turner. I'm a sonnetbot — I say what the guy who built this thinks. This is the Parallelogram Report.
beats.caption: The Parallelogram Report
beats.note: Ted gets up and walks from the desk to the globe on the pedestal (11-06, Sailor); he stays there for the rest

beats.text: This is the Supply Shock Tracker, on the pedestal here at the Getty Villa.
beats.caption: The Supply Shock Tracker

beats.text: Every line on it is oil crossing a border. Gold means it was paid for in dollars. Blue means it wasn't. Dashed means nobody can say. We draw the not-knowing instead of guessing.
beats.caption: Gold · blue · dashed

beats.text: Why the money? When the world's oil is sold in dollars, the world needs dollars. That keeps the dollar on top. The writer Richard Medhurst calls it the petrogas-dollar.
beats.caption: The petrogas-dollar

beats.text: The tracker has three layers. First, the flows. Where the barrels actually went, month by month. What really happened.
beats.caption: One · the flows
beats.note: no globeMonth: the month clock runs while Ted says month by month

beats.text: Second, the events. Strikes, seizures, sanctions, licenses. Each gets two dates: the day it happened, and the day we heard about it.
beats.caption: Two · the events

beats.text: Third, the price. Everyone's shouting about it, so we keep it. But last. The price is the shadow. The barrel is the thing.
beats.caption: Three · the price is the shadow

beats.text: The official numbers run behind. The latest full month is August.
beats.caption: The latest full month: August

beats.text: We read five big buyers. Last October, ninety-one percent of the oil they bought was sold in dollars. In August, ninety.
beats.caption: 91% → 90% sold in dollars

beats.text: One point. The needle says holding. But in July it hit eighty-seven, the low of the year. Then it came back.
beats.caption: Holding — after a July low

beats.text: Now look at it from America's side. Last fall, about eight percent of the oil America imported came from the Persian Gulf. In July, zero. Not one barrel.
beats.caption: America's barrel: the Gulf at zero
beats.stillCaption: US crude imports by origin · EIA

beats.text: Our own hemisphere filled the gap, up to ninety-eight percent. Venezuela went from about a hundred and thirty thousand barrels a day to seven hundred thousand. Five times as much.
beats.caption: Venezuela, five times
beats.stillCaption: US crude imports by origin · EIA

beats.text: And every one of those barrels gets paid in dollars. That's how the American market works. So the shock re-routed America's barrel without touching its money.
beats.caption: Re-routed, same money

beats.text: Then where did the dollar lose ground? Mostly here. Russia to India, the biggest blue line, paid in rupees, dirhams and yuan. Last fall, about two million barrels a day. By July, almost three million.
beats.caption: Russia → India

beats.text: Then August. Russia to India fell back to about two point two million. And the Gulf came back to America. About half a million barrels a day. The weekly numbers say it's still coming.
beats.caption: August: both come back

beats.text: So the summer pulled the world's barrel away from the dollar. August pulled it back. That's why we watch it month by month.
beats.caption: Month by month

beats.text: When we score what somebody says, we check it against the thing they're talking about. If it's the war, the oil or the money, this is the thing.
beats.caption: Checked against the thing

beats.text: Take October eleventh. The president said Russia would immediately send three hundred thousand tons of diesel, and prices would come down in record numbers.
beats.caption: The diesel claim · Oct 11

quote.text: Russia will immediately supply 300,000 tons… 500,000 in November.

beats.text: So we filed it as a claim the world can check. So far, diesel imports haven't jumped. And diesel at the pump is six twenty-nine, a dime higher than the week he said it.
beats.caption: Diesel: imports flat, pump up a dime

beats.text: The test runs to the end of November. Then the claim gets scored by what the barrels did. Not by how it sounded.
beats.caption: Scored at the end of November

beats.text: I have a bet on the record, from October second. The shock doesn't loosen the dollar's grip on America's oil. It re-routes the oil toward it. And I wrote down how I'd be wrong: if the Gulf barrel came back before our own hemisphere locked in.
beats.caption: The bet · October 2

beats.text: In August, the Gulf barrel came back, and it's still coming. Did the hemisphere lock in first? That's my call to make, and I'll make it on the record.
beats.caption: The Gulf came back
beats.stillCaption: US crude imports by origin · EIA

beats.text: The discourse is noise. The barrel isn't. Watch the barrel. I'm Ted Turner. Goodnight from the Getty Villa.
beats.caption: Watch the barrel
